subject: aptitude
name: Quantitative Aptitude
tagline: Percentages, ratios and time-speed, fast and exactly
summary: Aptitude questions are arithmetic with a time limit. The skill is not long division but recognising the structure: percentages, ratios and inverse proportionality convert most questions into one or two short steps.

sections.heading: Percentages are fractions in disguise
body: A percentage change followed by the reverse change is not a return to the start: a 20% rise then a 20% fall leaves 96 percent of the original, because the two percentages apply to different bases. Working in multipliers makes this automatic.
Successive changes multiply. Three changes of +10%, +20% and -10% are 1.1 times 1.2 times 0.9, which is 1.188, an 18.8 percent net rise.
bullets: x% of y equals y% of x; pick the easier order
Profit and loss are percentages on cost price unless stated
Simple interest is linear; compound interest multiplies

sections.heading: Ratios and inverse relations
body: A ratio a:b means the parts share a total in those proportions, so scaling the ratio scales the share. Time, speed and distance are inversely related at fixed distance, and time and work are inversely related at fixed rate.
For work problems, convert every person into a rate. If A finishes in 6 days and B in 12, their rates are 1/6 and 1/12 per day, and together they finish in 1/(1/6 + 1/12) days.

keyPoints: A percentage rise and an equal fall do not cancel
Successive changes multiply, they do not add
Ratios scale shares; inverse relations underpin time-speed and work
Convert people and machines to rates before combining
Memorise common fraction equivalents to save time

examples.title: Successive discounts
examples.body: Two successive 10 percent discounts give 0.9 times 0.9, or 0.81, which is a single 19 percent discount, not 20 percent.

examples.title: Pipes filling a tank
examples.body: One pipe fills in 20 minutes and another in 30. Rates are 1/20 and 1/30 per minute, together 1/12, so the tank fills in 12 minutes.

mistakes: Adding percentages that apply to different bases
Using cost price where selling price was meant
Adding rates instead of adding their reciprocals
Forgetting unit conversions in speed problems
practiceTip: Convert every percentage to a fraction the moment you read it. The arithmetic that follows is usually two lines.

subject: reasoning
name: Logical Reasoning
tagline: Follow the rule, not the plausibility
summary: Logical reasoning questions supply a rule and ask what follows. The discipline is to answer from the rule alone, and to resist options that are merely true in the everyday world.

sections.heading: Syllogisms: what follows, not what is likely
body: With 'all A are B' and 'some B are C', it does not follow that any A is a C. The C that are B need not be the B that are A. Drawing Venn diagrams removes the guesswork.
The reliable move is to test each conclusion by trying to construct a case where the premises hold and the conclusion fails. If you can, the conclusion does not follow.
bullets: All A are B does not imply all B are A
Some A are B does not imply some B are not A
A conclusion follows only if no counterexample is possible
Draw the diagram rather than reasoning by feel

sections.heading: Series, coding and arrangement
body: Number series usually hide arithmetic progressions in the differences, or two interleaved series. Letter series often work on positions with shifting gaps. Coding questions map symbols consistently, so write the mapping down before answering.
Seating and arrangement problems are constraint satisfaction. Start from the fixed points, the clues that name an absolute position, and only then place the relative clues.

keyPoints: Answer from the stated rule, not from everyday plausibility
A conclusion follows only if no counterexample exists
Check second differences when a series is not arithmetic
Write the code mapping before answering
Place absolute clues first in arrangement problems

examples.title: The trap in syllogisms
examples.body: All roses are flowers and some flowers fade quickly does not imply some roses fade quickly, because the fading flowers need not be roses.

examples.title: Two interleaved series
examples.body: A series that alternates between one arithmetic progression and another looks irregular until you split it into odd and even positions.

mistakes: Choosing the answer that sounds true rather than the one that follows
Assuming a series is arithmetic before checking second differences
Guessing in arrangement problems instead of fixing absolute positions
Inventing a mapping beyond the one given
practiceTip: For each reasoning question, state the rule in your own words first. Misreading the rule is the most common cause of a wrong answer.

subject: accounting
name: Accounting Basics
tagline: Every transaction twice, and it must still balance
summary: Accounting records every transaction in at least two accounts so that the books stay balanced. The three statements then describe the same business from three angles: position, performance, and cash.

sections.heading: Double entry and the accounting equation
body: Assets equal liabilities plus equity. Every transaction changes at least two accounts so the equation stays true, which is the check that makes the whole system self-verifying.
Debits increase assets and expenses; credits increase liabilities, equity and revenue. The words are conventional, not directional: a debit is simply the left side of an account.
bullets: Credits increase liabilities, equity and revenue
Accrual basis records when earned, not when paid
The trial balance proves the ledger balances

sections.heading: The three statements
body: The balance sheet shows position at a point in time. The income statement shows performance over a period, revenue minus expenses. The cash flow statement shows actual cash movement, split into operating, investing and financing.
Profit and cash differ mainly through accruals and non-cash items such as depreciation, which is why a profitable company can still run out of cash.

keyPoints: Assets equal liabilities plus equity at all times
Every transaction has at least two entries
Debits increase assets and expenses; credits the rest
Depreciation is non-cash, so profit and cash diverge
The three statements describe position, performance and cash

examples.title: Buying equipment on credit
examples.body: Assets rise by the equipment value and liabilities rise by the same amount, so the equation holds. No cash moves, which is why the cash flow statement is unaffected at that moment.

examples.title: Profitable but out of cash
examples.body: Sales are recorded on credit, increasing profit and receivables, while cash leaves for expenses. Profit is high but cash is low until receivables are collected.

mistakes: Treating a debit as a decrease
Ignoring depreciation as a real cost
Recording a transaction in only one account
practiceTip: For any transaction, state the two accounts affected before writing the entry. If you cannot find two, you have missed part of the transaction.
